chunks: ʿAlī ibn Ibrāhīm, from his father, from Yaḥyā ibn Abī ʿImrān, from Yūnus, from Bakkār ibn Bakr, from Mūsā ibn Ashyam, who said:

I was with Abī ʿAbdillāh عليه السلام, and a man asked him about a verse from the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so he informed him about it. Then another person came in and asked him about that same verse, and he informed him contrary to what he had informed the first one. Because of that, there entered into me whatever Allah willed, until it was as though my heart were being cut open with knives.

So I said to myself: I left Abū Qatādah in al-Shām, who does not err even regarding the wāw and the like of it, and I came to this one who makes all these mistakes. While I was in that state, another person entered and asked him about that same verse, and he informed him contrary to what he had informed me and what he had informed my two companions. Then my soul became calm, and I knew that this was from him as taqiyyah.
He said: Then he turned toward me and said to me: O Ibn Ashyam, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, delegated authority to Sulaymān ibn Dāwūd, so He said:
“This is Our gift; so give or withhold without account.”
And He delegated authority to His Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله, so He said:
“Whatever the Messenger gives you, take it; and whatever he forbids you from, refrain.”
So whatever was delegated to the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله has indeed been delegated to us.

key_terms.آيَةٍ: a verse from the Qur'an being asked about
key_terms.الرَّسُولُ: the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
key_terms.تَقِيَّةٌ: dissimulation for protection in circumstances requiring concealment
key_terms.عَطَاؤُنَا: Our gift, referring to divine bestowal
key_terms.فَانْتَهُوا: refrain or desist from what is forbidden
key_terms.كِتَابِ اللَّهِ: the Book of Allah, meaning the Qur'an

ai.seo_question: How does this hadith explain taqiyyah and the delegated authority of the Imam in interpreting religion?
ai.summary: This hadith shows that Imam al-Ṣādiq عليه السلام sometimes gave differing outward answers out of taqiyyah, and that such variation did not arise from error. It then grounds the authority of the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم and the Ahl al-Bayt عليهم السلام in Qur'anic delegation, indicating that what Allah delegated to His Messenger صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم was also delegated to them.
